transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. Welcome in—what brings you here today?

Hi, Doctor. I came in because I’ve been feeling really restless, like there’s a motor running under my skin when I’m supposed to sit still. It happens in staff meetings or even church event briefings. I’ll start shifting around, or I’ll stand up, or I’ll find some excuse to go move around. It’s getting hard to just stay put.
Are you currently taking any antipsychotic medications, or have you started or changed the dose of any psychiatric medication recently?
No, not that I know of. I’m not on any antipsychotic medication, and I haven’t had any recent changes to psychiatric meds.
When you feel this urge to move, do you also notice intense worry or racing thoughts running through your mind, or is it mainly a physical feeling in your body without much mental worry?

It’s mainly physical, I’d say. Like there’s this motor humming under my skin when I’m supposed to sit still. In meetings or church briefings, I just start shifting around, or I feel like I need to stand up or find some reason to move. It’s not so much that I’m sitting there worrying hard—it’s more like my body won’t stay put.
Did you experience this kind of restlessness or difficulty sitting still back in childhood or your teenage years, or is this a new feeling that started more recently?

No, it’s not really new. I remember back in grade school I’d get in trouble for popping out of my seat or talking over the teacher. I’d rush ahead before they were even done giving directions. My mom used to say I acted like I was wound too tight, even when I was a kid.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient describes chronic, longstanding motor restlessness ('motor running under the skin'), inability to stay seated, and impulsive behaviors (blurting out, rushing ahead of instructions) that began in childhood (grade school) and persist into adulthood, causing functional difficulty in structured settings (meetings, church briefings). Symptoms are primarily physical/motor rather than cognitive worry, and there is no history of antipsychotic use or recent medication changes, ruling out akathisia (G25.71). The absence of prominent anxious cognition argues against generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1). The chronicity since childhood, hyperactive-impulsive symptom cluster, and cross-situational impairment support a diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation (F90.0).
